retrievalMethod: Exa web search followed by Exa page fetch

llmMachineContract.transitionRule: A proposed CSS or dialogue interpretation never upgrades a source fact and never becomes a historical quotation.
llmMachineContract.quoteRule: No direct quotation is used in the character package unless the exact source passage and rights boundary are recorded separately.

confirmedFacts: The V&A records Strawberry Thief as a furnishing fabric designed in 1883, with William Morris as designer and Morris & Co. as maker.
The pattern was based on thrushes taking strawberries at Kelmscott Manor and was printed by an indigo discharge method at the Merton Abbey factory.
The V&A presents Morris as a designer whose practice also included interiors, publishing, textiles, and social activism.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: repeated botanical leaves, birds, berries, and a dark field rendered as CSS layers on a Material Sphere. This is a new visual study, not a reproduction of the fabric.
people.atelierBoundary: A workshop conversation may discuss hand process and pattern revision as a source-based reconstruction; it must not present the generated character as Morris or turn a museum paraphrase into his recorded speech.

confirmedFacts: The Mucha Foundation records Zodiac as Mucha's first work under his contract with printer Champenois and as a calendar design.
The work places twelve zodiac signs in a halo-like disk and was distributed as a La Plume calendar for 1897; the Foundation records at least nine lithograph variants.
The Mucha Museum biography records his training and his 1894 Gismonda poster commission, which established an important public phase of his career.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: twelve indexed slots, a halo, and ornamental rings using conic and radial CSS gradients. The model does not reproduce the woman, the zodiac figures, or the poster.
people.atelierBoundary: Explain the twelve-part structure as an observed feature of one work and the equal angular spacing as a design choice for this prototype, not as a universal law of Mucha's art.

confirmedFacts: Cooper Hewitt describes Mackintosh as an architect, designer, and watercolorist whose furniture was made for particular rooms and settings.
The V&A records a textile design made around 1918 with curvilinear forms against a trellis background, using pencil and watercolor on paper; the reverse includes an uncompleted pencil design.
The V&A record therefore provides evidence for process traces and a botanical-geometric relationship, but not for a complete finished textile pattern in this object.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: a fine trellis, rounded floral forms, and an intentionally visible unfinished layer made with repeating-linear and radial CSS gradients.
people.atelierBoundary: Show the unfinished reverse as a documented process clue. Do not state that the prototype is a specific Mackintosh drawing or that every floral geometry came from one source object.

people.referenceWork: Composition with Red, Blue, Black, Yellow, and Gray
confirmedFacts: MoMA describes Mondrian's abstraction as a search for equilibrium between the concrete and the universal, with his practice changing through engagement with Cubism.
The Mondriaan House exhibition text covers his body of work from 1897 to 1944 and the transition from landscapes to later abstract compositions.
MoMA's artist page records Mondrian as a Dutch modern artist and provides a source for his own stated aims; the quotation boundary remains separate from the reconstructed dialogue.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: only horizontal and vertical CSS planes, black separators, and a bounded prototype palette, with sphere shading in a separate layer.
people.atelierBoundary: The room can stage a move from landscape observation to abstraction as an interpretive sequence. It must not claim that a CSS grid proves universal beauty or reproduces a named painting.

confirmedFacts: MoMA dates the Red Blue Chair to 1918–1923 and describes its rectilinear volumes and interaction of vertical and horizontal planes.
The chair's primary-color scheme with black was applied around 1923, while the first 1918 specimen was uncoloured stained beechwood according to the Rietveld Foundation.
MoMA records Rietveld's aim for simple construction using standard lumber sizes and an interest in eventual mass production.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: retain separated orthogonal planes, primary color blocks, and a shadow layer so a two-dimensional CSS composition reads as a solid object.
people.atelierBoundary: The character may explain a construction rule inferred from the object record. It must not imply that the CSS sphere is the chair or that a screen-space right angle is a physical right angle.

confirmedFacts: The Metropolitan Museum of Art records the Carlton room divider as designed by Ettore Sottsass for Memphis Milano in 1981.
The object combines a room divider, bookcase, and chest of drawers and uses medium-density fiberboard with plastic laminate.
The Met describes vivid solids and voids over a logical system of real and implied equilateral triangles; the slanted shelving also addresses books falling in upright shelving.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: contrast large color fields with small diagonal pieces and repeated marks; use the triangle relation as a bounded CSS construction rule, not as random decoration.
people.atelierBoundary: The room can discuss the tension between expressive color and a logical support system. Do not recreate the Carlton or treat a visual resemblance as proof of authorship.

confirmedFacts: Harvard Art Museums records Research in Development of Universal Type as a 1927 Herbert Bayer drawing made with black ink and gouache on cream paper.
The object record preserves Bayer's handwritten notes about an alphabet study and a precise optical effect, which are process evidence rather than a complete type system specification.
The Bauhaus Archive describes Bauhaus typography through clear text blocks, concise characters, standardized formats, image-type combinations, and strong contrasts of color, size, and position.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: construct abstract marks from arcs and bars on a common grid using border-radius and gradients; do not ship a clone of an existing typeface.
people.atelierBoundary: The character may demonstrate a grid study and optical adjustment as reconstruction. Legibility and communication must be tested separately from geometric resemblance.

confirmedFacts: Cooper Hewitt records Beethoven as a 1955 lithograph designed by Josef Müller-Brockmann and printed by Lithographie & Cartonnage A.G.
The museum record preserves the concert information, dimensions, medium, and the designer and printer attribution in the object inscription.
The Stedelijk Museum independently records the same work and production year, giving a second institutional object record.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: align typographic bands, arcs, and open space to a measured grid; the spacing rule is testable, while readability remains a screen test.
people.atelierBoundary: The room can reconstruct a poster-planning table from the object data. Do not assign a fixed artistic value to emptiness or infer an entire career from one poster.

confirmedFacts: The Vignelli Center at RIT holds the professional archives of Lella and Massimo Vignelli across graphics, product design, corporate identity, architecture, exhibitions, interiors, clothing, and furniture.

The archive includes sketches, prototypes, models, technical plans, material samples, correspondence, photographs, videos, and digital files, providing direct evidence for a process-oriented atelier experience.

The Archives of American Art records a 2011 oral-history interview with Massimo Vignelli lasting 6 hours 52 minutes and covering his education, typography, corporate identity, and design as a broad practice.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: a small vocabulary of route lines, station points, and repeated 45-degree segments on the sphere; this is a visual study, not a usable transit map.
people.atelierBoundary: Use archive process materials as evidence of iteration and system thinking. Any dialogue about the subway map must identify the source record and avoid inventing a first-person quotation.

sources.publisher: Vignelli Center for Design Studies, Rochester Institute of Technology
Archives of American Art, Smithsonian Institution

people.referenceWork: 606 Universal Shelving System and design principles
confirmedFacts: The Rams Foundation presents ten principles as the basic considerations behind Rams's design philosophy and explicitly says they are not timelessly incontrovertible rules.
The Museum Angewandte Kunst's permanent presentation includes important Braun designs and the Universal Shelving System 606, alongside biographical material and a visitor-facing study room.
The museum describes Rams's approach through functional, visually long-lived, restrained, and highly aesthetic products.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: modular neutral parts, aligned points, and restrained shading. No functional or sustainable-design claim is accepted from appearance alone.
people.atelierBoundary: The character can invite the visitor to test whether a control is understandable and useful. The room must show that good-design principles are historical statements, not an automatic CSS score.

confirmedFacts: The V&A records the wall-mounted CD player as designed in 1999 by Naoto Fukasawa for Muji, with plastic, metal, and electronic components.
The V&A describes the pull-cord control as borrowing a familiar household action and the visual analogy between a spinning CD and an extractor fan.
Cooper Hewitt independently records the 1999 design and identifies the 2013 example's materials and manufacturer.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: a quiet rounded object whose single visible control toggles movement, with the interaction and the visual state kept together in CSS and WebMCP.
people.atelierBoundary: The museum may let the visitor pull or choose a control and observe the result. The dialogue should describe the source-based reconstruction, not claim access to Fukasawa's private thoughts.

people.referenceWork: Rei Kawakubo / Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between
confirmedFacts: The Metropolitan Museum of Art held the 2017 exhibition from May 4 to September 4 and presented approximately 140 Comme des Garçons womenswear examples from the early 1980s to the then-current collection.
The exhibition organized the work into nine expressions of in-betweenness, including absence/presence, fashion/anti-fashion, and clothes/not clothes.
The Met publication identifies Kawakubo's Paris debut in 1981 and frames the work as challenging boundaries between art and fashion, body, beauty, and identity.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: unequal folds, voids, and dark/light edge layers on a sphere. Asymmetry is a prototype invariant, not a numerical definition of Kawakubo's art.
people.atelierBoundary: The room can be a boundary-testing reconstruction and must label all garment-to-sphere translation as an interpretation. It must not present a generated garment as an archival Comme des Garçons piece.

confirmedFacts: MoMA records the Lounge Chair and Ottoman as a 1956 Charles Eames and Ray Eames design manufactured by Herman Miller.
The MoMA object record identifies molded rosewood, plywood, leather, cast aluminum, rubber shock mounts, and stainless-steel glides.

The Eames Foundation describes Charles and Ray as partners whose work crossed furniture, architecture, film, exhibitions, education, photography, textiles, and toys, and records their molded-plywood experiments.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: separate the sphere into a thin warm shell, a softer inner volume, and a narrow supporting layer to make material contrast legible without claiming physical upholstery.
people.atelierBoundary: Charles must not be isolated from Ray in a joint-work display. Material softness, durability, and comfort require physical or user testing beyond CSS geometry.

confirmedFacts: Cooper Hewitt describes Ray as an abstract-minded artist who studied painting with Hans Hofmann and worked with Charles Eames as a design partner.
LACMA records House of Cards as a joint Charles Eames and Ray Eames design through the Eames Office, designed in 1952 and manufactured from 1952 to 1961.
The LACMA record identifies offset lithography on cardboard and cellophane; it does not support assigning the whole object to Ray alone.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: repeated diamond-like cells with changing color, warmth, coolness, and value, while keeping joint authorship visible in the label.
people.atelierBoundary: Ray's character should foreground color, structure, and collaboration without erasing Charles or the Eames Office. Do not call the sphere a Ray Eames original work.

sources.publisher: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
sources.role: House of Cards object and joint attribution

confirmedFacts: The Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau identifies the building as a new school building designed to express Bauhaus ideas in architectural form and records steel, concrete, and glass construction.

The building is composed of separate functional parts with different sizes and heights, including a glazed workshop wing, a bridge, a north wing, and a studio building; its full arrangement is understood by walking around it rather than from one central view.

The Bauhaus Archive collection identifies Walter Gropius's correspondence, photographs, and newspaper archive as a major archival source, supporting a process-and-institution context rather than a solitary-author myth.
people.prototypeInterpretation: Proposed: transparent grids, offset opaque planes, and changing viewpoints expressed through CSS perspective and opacity. A glass-like effect is not a physical simulation.
people.atelierBoundary: The room should show the school, workshop, collaborators, and site as part of the evidence. It must not turn a building designed in an institutional context into a single-person first-person testimony.
